reading: The David Rumsey Historical Map Collection gathers, preserves, catalogs and shares an unusually large collection of historical maps, with particular strength in the Americas and material ranging from the sixteenth to the twenty-first century. It treats maps as both historical evidence and visual inventions: close inspection can reveal poetic annotations, decorative conventions, imagined skies and changing ideas of places. Its vocabulary is that of atlases, planispheres, globes, sheets, cartouches, catalog records, georeferencing and map coverage. It cares about open access, detailed images, provenance and making old maps useful through new technology. What distinguishes it is the tension between physical artifacts and their many digital lives: sixty sheets become one world, old and modern geography can be overlaid, and the same collection can be explored as a globe, a searchable region or a tiny detail. The connected Japanese collection and publications extend that curiosity beyond a single place or medium.

enemies.idea: The Sheet Stitcher scuttles on sixty articulated manuscript panels, joining their edges around a crew until every escape leads back to the center of the 1587 planisphere.
enemies.why: Crews can sever seams and rearrange a world-sized trap while the machine hurriedly stitches it back together.

enemies.idea: A georeferencing tick plants paired control points in old and modern ground, then drags everything between them into alignment, bending streets and pulling travelers sideways.
enemies.why: Its anchor points make a visible puzzle: move or break them to restore a safe route.

enemies.idea: Coverage hounds sweep a region and rank every moving object as a map result; the closer a traveler gets to their chosen area, the more hounds converge.
enemies.why: A search for useful coverage becomes a pursuit that players can redirect by changing the area being searched.

enemies.idea: A railroad-distance engine lays down tracks that shorten its own journey and lengthen everyone else's, announcing each new distance as if it were an objective measurement.
enemies.why: The landscape becomes a manipulable route puzzle, with the enemy's distance figures revealing its next move.

enemies.idea: The Cetus plotter casts points of cold light across the ground; when it connects enough stars, a mechanical sea monster rises along the lines and pursues anything that breaks the constellation.
enemies.why: The crew can interrupt the drawing or lure the completed creature into crossing its own lines.

enemies.idea: A relief engraver unfolds the thirty-one sheets of the Kingdom of Naples into sharp ridges, raising a miniature landscape until it becomes an impassable mechanical range.
enemies.why: Its terrain-building attack gives the crew cover as well as obstacles; individual sheets can be folded down.

enemies.idea: The river-chart dredger follows the 1858 Lower Mississippi on a rolling strip of map, insisting the channel still runs where its chart says and carving that route through whatever stands there now.
enemies.why: Its old course is readable in advance, letting a crew race ahead to divert the strip or prepare an ambush.

enemies.idea: A verse-mill has swallowed the two-line annotation on the Texas plains map. It prints new couplets that turn each place it names into a stretching, empty plain.
enemies.why: The crew can interrupt a line before its final place-name or feed the machine an unlikely rhyme.

enemies.idea: A globe of the Moon's morphology sheds crater-shaped drones that try to stamp matching basins into the floor, fitting the local terrain to their mosaic.
enemies.why: The impact patterns reveal where the next crater will land and can be used to expose buried routes.

enemies.idea: A terrestrial globe roller spins its surface beneath itself, bringing a different coastline into contact with the ground every revolution and trying to make the room match it.
enemies.why: Its rotation telegraphs a changing battlefield and creates a chance to wedge the globe at a useful coast.

enemies.idea: A catalog bailiff assigns every traveler a media summary, date and title, then shelves anyone whose record it considers incomplete in a rolling stack of map cases.
enemies.why: Its classification rules can be exploited with contradictory descriptions and swapped labels.

enemies.idea: The abbreviation collector bites references down to cryptic initials, then mistakes anything sharing those initials for the same object and clamps the objects together.
enemies.why: A seemingly scholarly nuisance becomes a physical matching puzzle with playful cases of mistaken identity.

enemies.idea: Sugoroku move-takers stamp numbered spaces on the floor and force travelers to advance or retreat according to the next roll; the swarm shortcuts between spaces it has already claimed.
enemies.why: A historical game becomes a contested board where players can alter the route and turn the rules against its makers.

enemies.idea: A city-atlas layerer drops four centuries of San Francisco maps over a room in rapid succession, building streets that exist only until the next sheet falls.
enemies.why: The changing layers create brief bridges and cover, rewarding timing and attention to each map.

enemies.idea: The atlas binder snaps shut around anything it finds between its covers, then releases duplicate paper-thin copies that patrol in formation.
enemies.why: Escaping the covers is urgent, while identifying the original among flimsy duplicates makes the follow-up encounter surprising.

enemies.idea: A surveyor of peaks and rivers stretches a metal measuring chain between the tallest and longest things nearby, forcibly rearranging them into a comparative diagram.
enemies.why: The chain becomes both a hazard and a tool for pulling the surveyor off balance.

enemies.idea: The contour double projects the mountain as seen from the forest and as seen across the plateau, attacking whenever the crew mistakes one view of Pico de Orizaba for the other.
enemies.why: Two perspectives of the same landmark create a spatial riddle with a clear tell.

enemies.idea: An accession swarm pours out of old catalog drawers in numbered waves, attempting to add every loose object to the collection and carry it away by accession number.
enemies.why: The crew can follow the numbering to recover stolen supplies or insert a decoy object into the procession.

enemies.idea: A celestial globe turns inside out, releasing mechanical star figures that keep their relative positions even as they chase, dragging each other around corners.
enemies.why: Their rigid constellation formation is dangerous in open spaces but awkward in narrow passages.

enemies.idea: A text-on-maps reader plucks place names off old sheets and pins them to the nearest living traveler; the swarm then navigates toward those people as if they were destinations.
enemies.why: Stolen names can be exchanged or attached to decoys, turning pursuit into a game of misdirection.

enemies.idea: A GIS time-layer machine stamps different dates onto neighboring patches of ground, letting its scouts slip between versions while trapping visitors at the seam.
enemies.why: A crew can learn the cycle and cross at the moment two layers agree.

enemies.idea: A facsimile globe makes a convincing copy of any route it rolls over, but reverses one crucial turn and sends its paper scouts to patrol the false route.
enemies.why: Comparing original and copy reveals the deception and gives the crew a way to send scouts elsewhere.

allies.idea: A volunteer georeferencer keeps a box of loose control points and helps crews pin an old sheet to the present without letting the swarm drag either one around.
allies.why: The ally gives players a practical way to stabilize warped ground and rewards finding reliable landmarks.

allies.idea: A free-access map keeper unfolds duplicate sheets for anyone who asks, leaving copies behind so a lost crew can find its way even after the original is seized.
allies.why: Sharing becomes a concrete advantage: every rescued copy can help a later traveler.

allies.idea: A detail scout studies the smallest marks on damaged maps and spots the odd cartographic convention that reveals where a larger swarm machine is vulnerable.
allies.why: Close looking becomes a source of actionable clues instead of background decoration.

allies.idea: A surviving cataloger records an object's title and provenance before the swarm can rename it, helping crews distinguish an original map from a misleading facsimile.
allies.why: Careful metadata offers a useful defense against the swarm's false copies.

allies.idea: A tactile atlas guide traces raised paths with a crew's hands when visual maps are unreliable, guiding them through shifting layers by touch.
allies.why: The 1837 atlas for blind readers inspires a different and cooperative way to navigate.

bosses.idea: The Grand Georeferencer is a walking archive of atlas cases, globe rings and survey arms. It believes every historical map must be true in the same place at once, and pulls whole eras into alignment around its control points. Break the anchors, then choose which conflicting sheet to ground long enough to reach its core.
bosses.why: It combines preservation, historical disagreement and modern overlay into a fight about choosing a stable route through incompatible worlds.

bosses.idea: The Sixty-Sheet World Engine unfolds a ten-foot planisphere into a rolling floor, then feeds it maps from every era to fill the gaps. Its seams open into separate regions; a crew must detach the sheet carrying its compass before the engine stitches itself into a closed world.
bosses.why: The collection's ambition to assemble a whole world becomes a spectacular, legible multi-stage encounter.

bosses.idea: The Universal Catalog is a many-drawered machine that captures maps and travelers alike, assigning every one a single authoritative title and place. It grows stronger when its records agree; returning conflicting dates, perspectives and versions to its drawers causes it to jam.
bosses.why: The collection's breadth and cataloging become a boss whose weakness is the rich multiplicity the archive exists to preserve.

events.idea: Two loose sheets from the sixty-sheet planisphere are being stitched edge to edge backwards. A crew can turn one before the seam closes and opens a route into a new region.
events.why: A small intervention turns a famous oversized map into a changing passage.

events.idea: A railroad-distance engine has marked a short walk as a hundred miles. Travelers can follow its rails to the measuring wheel and reset the distance before a supply cart runs out of time.
events.why: The absurd measurement has a practical consequence and a visible mechanism to fix.

events.idea: A star plate has lost one point of Cetus; a loose lamp rolls toward a drain while the unfinished creature searches blindly for it.
events.why: The crew can complete the figure, hide the star or use its light to navigate.

events.idea: A georeferencing anchor has slipped, leaving an old road hovering just above a modern one. A trapped cart needs the two aligned long enough to cross.
events.why: A brief rescue makes the overlay mechanic tangible before a larger encounter.

events.idea: A Sugoroku die rolls into a corridor and stamps a winding sequence of spaces behind it. Anyone who reaches the last space before the die stops finds a cache of rescued map fragments.
events.why: A passing crew gets an optional race through a game-board landscape.

events.idea: A river chart is unrolling into a dry hallway, with little machine boats following its printed channel. One boat carries a map case that the crew needs to retrieve without tearing the chart.
events.why: The tiny convoy offers a delicate moving-target challenge instead of a fight.

events.idea: Two views of the same mountain point in different directions. A broken survey machine asks to be turned until its plateau view and forest view agree on the peak.
events.why: The reward comes from understanding that a landmark changes shape with perspective.

events.idea: A drawer spills catalog cards with titles separated from their dates. Reuniting the pairs before an accession swarm arrives reveals which map case contains a safe route.
events.why: Cataloging becomes a quick physical sorting task under pressure.

events.idea: The two lines of a map annotation have drifted apart across a mechanical plain. Bring them together and the expanding blank ground contracts, uncovering a buried doorway.
events.why: A rare poetic detail gives players a poetic solution to an environmental obstacle.

events.idea: A map keeper offers free copies of a safe route, but the copier has mixed an obsolete layer into every other sheet. The crew can compare landmarks and mark the misleading copies before others take them.
events.why: Open access becomes a chance to help future travelers while practicing careful map reading.

events.idea: A globe rolls to a stop with a coastline facing the floor. Lift it and turn it to the matching coastline on a nearby sheet to unlock a stranded scout's case.
events.why: A physical globe-to-map comparison makes geography tactile.

events.idea: A stack of city maps keeps replacing a bridge with different streets as the years change. A crew can time a crossing or hold one sheet in place for a slower companion.
events.why: Changing urban history creates a short cooperative timing challenge.

events.idea: A relief sheet has buckled into a miniature mountain range around a dropped tool. Flattening the correct section retrieves it, but folds up a different route.
events.why: A simple choice makes the paper terrain feel responsive and useful.

events.idea: A cataloger and a facsimile globe disagree about which of two maps is original. The crew can compare their records and a tiny copied imperfection to return each to its proper case.
events.why: A low-stakes mystery celebrates originals, copies and close observation.

events.idea: A measuring chain has snagged a mountain diagram and a river diagram together. Unhooking it frees a path, but sends the chain recoiling toward a pile of fragile maps.
events.why: A comparative chart creates a quick rescue with a satisfying physical consequence.
